description: Conversational learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

article.title: Dark Patterns Work Too Well: Why Good Design Can Be Unethical
article.author: Emma Rodriguez

cards.title: Confirmshaming Weaponizes Guilt
cards.subtitle: 'No thanks, I hate saving money.' The decline button shames you.
body: The design frames your choice as a character flaw. Every dismissal becomes a tiny shame event.
Notice when a design tries to make you feel bad for saying no.
cards.takeaway: Decline options that shame you are a design choice, not an accident.

cards.title: Hidden Costs at Checkout
cards.subtitle: The price was $20. Now it's $34.50. You're too invested to quit.
body: Fees appear at the last moment. You've already spent time deciding.
The sunk cost fallacy is built into the flow. Last-minute changes are often intentional.
cards.takeaway: Hidden costs exploit the effort you've already invested.

cards.title: Easy In, Hard Out
cards.subtitle: Signing up: one click. Unsubscribing: password, confirmation, guilt trip.
body: Friction-free signup, friction-heavy exit. The asymmetry is intentional.
Every barrier to exit increases retention numbers.
cards.takeaway: Easy in, hard out is a common design pattern.

cards.title: Pre-Checked Boxes
cards.subtitle: You ordered a book. Also apparently: insurance, newsletter, and expedited shipping.
body: Defaults are powerful. Pre-checked boxes capture your inattention.

• Most users accept extras they didn't choose
• Opting out requires reading every line
cards.takeaway: Pre-checked boxes are designed to capture inattention.

cards.title: Free Trial Forgetting
cards.subtitle: You forgot to cancel. Now you've paid for six months.
body: Free trials require payment upfront. The trial ends silently. Charges begin automatically.
Forgetting is literally the business model. Set a reminder before you sign up.
cards.takeaway: Free trials often rely on you forgetting to cancel.

cards.title: Privacy Defaults to Maximum Sharing
cards.subtitle: Opting out requires fourteen toggles across three screens.
body: Privacy controls exist but default to maximum sharing.
The design makes privacy the expensive, time-consuming option.
cards.takeaway: Privacy often requires active effort to protect.

cards.title: Scarcity Timers Are Often Fake
cards.subtitle: 'Only 2 left!' The timer resets after every page load.
body: Artificial urgency bypasses rational thinking. The scarcity is fake; the pressure is real.
When you see a countdown, ask whether it's genuine.
cards.takeaway: Scarcity and timers are often manufactured, not genuine.

cards.title: Infinite Scroll Removes Stopping Points
cards.subtitle: No end, no page two—just more content forever.
body: Pagination used to give natural exits. Infinite scroll removes them.
The design puts the decision to stop entirely on you.
cards.takeaway: Infinite scroll is designed to keep you scrolling.

cards.title: Bait and Switch
cards.subtitle: You clicked 'Download.' It was actually 'Start free trial and download.'
body: Button labels shift between preview and action.
The switch happens at the moment you're already committed to clicking.
cards.takeaway: Button labels can change between attention and action.

cards.title: Roach Motel
cards.subtitle: Signing up: one click. Deleting account: email support, wait three days.
body: Entry is frictionless. Exit is deliberately obstructed.
Before you sign up, check how hard it is to leave.
cards.takeaway: Easy signup and hard exit is a retention strategy.

cards.title: Social Proof Can Be Fake
cards.subtitle: 'Join 50,000 satisfied customers!' The company launched last month.
body: Testimonials and star ratings get inflated or purchased.
Numbers are persuasive and easy to fabricate. Take them with a grain of salt.
cards.takeaway: Social proof can be manufactured; verification is rare.
